section.heading: 15.4. Applications of Double Integrals
section.paragraph: We have already seen one application of double integrals: computing volumes. Another geometric application is finding areas of surfaces and this will be done in the next section. In this section we explore physical applications such as computing mass, electric charge, center of mass, and moment of inertia. We will see that these physical ideas are also important when applied to probability density functions of two random variables.
section.heading: Density and Mass
section.paragraph: In Section 8.3 we were able to use single integrals to compute moments and the center of mass of a thin plate or lamina with constant density. But now, equipped with the double integral, we can consider a lamina with variable density. Suppose the lamina occupies a region $$D$$ of the $$xy$$ -plane and its density (in units of mass per unit area) at a point $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ in $$D$$ is given by $$\rho\left( {x,y} \right)$$ , where $$\rho$$ is a continuous function on $$D$$ . This means that
$$\rho\left( {x,y} \right) = \lim\frac{\Delta m}{\Delta A}$$

where $$\Delta m$$ and $$\Delta A$$ are the mass and area of a small rectangle that contains $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ and the limit is taken as the dimensions of the rectangle approach 0. (See Figure 1.)

image.alt: Details A rectangular grid, a closed curve, a shaded region, a square, and a point are graphed in the first quadrant of the x y coordinate plane. An irregular closed curve is drawn in the first quadrant within a rectangular grid such that its extreme points touch the sides of the grid. The region within the curve is shaded. One of the cells of the grid within the curve is shaded with a different color. An enlarged view of the cell shows a square with a point within. The square is labeled r_(i j) and the point is labeled (x^*_(i j), y^*_(i j)).

section.paragraph: To find the total mass $$m$$ of the lamina we divide a rectangle $$R$$ containing $$D$$ into subrectangles $$R_{ij}$$ of the same size (as in Figure 2) and consider $$\rho\left( {x,y} \right)$$ to be $$0$$ outside $$D$$ . If we choose a point $$({x_{ij}^{*},y_{ij}^{*}})$$ in $$R_{\mathit{ij}}$$ , then the mass of the part of the lamina that occupies $$R_{ij}$$ is approximately $$\rho{({x_{ij}^{*},y_{ij}^{*}})}\Delta A$$ , where $$\Delta A$$ is the area of $$R_{ij}$$ . If we add all such masses, we get an approximation to the total mass:
$$m \approx \sum\limits_{i = 1}^{k}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{l}{\rho{({x_{ij}^{*},y_{ij}^{*}})}\Delta A}}$$

figure.caption: The mass of each subrectangle $$R_{\mathit{ij}}$$ is approximated by $$\rho(x_{ij}^{*},y_{ij}^{*})\Delta A$$ .

section.paragraph: If we now increase the number of subrectangles, we obtain the total mass $$m$$ of the lamina as the limiting value of the approximations:
$$m = \lim\limits_{k,l\rightarrow\infty}\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{k}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{l}{\rho{({x_{ij}^{*},y_{ij}^{*}})}\Delta A =}}{\iint\limits_{D}{\rho\left( {x,y} \right)dA}}$$

Physicists also consider other types of density that can be treated in the same manner. For example, if an electric charge is distributed over a region $$D$$ and the charge density (in units of charge per unit area) is given by $$\sigma\left( {x,y} \right)$$ at a point $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ in $$D$$ , then the total electric charge $$Q$$ is given by
$$Q = {\iint\limits_{D}\sigma}\left( {x,y} \right)dA$$

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: Charge is distributed over the triangular region $$D$$ in Figure 3 so that the charge density at $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ is $$\sigma\left( {x,y} \right) = xy$$ , measured in coulombs per square meter $$(C \slash m^{2})$$ . Find the total charge.

image.alt: Details A triangle, a shaded region, and a line segment with an arrowhead are graphed in the x y coordinate plane. The triangle is a right triangle with its vertices at (1, 1), (1,0), and (0, 1). The top side of the triangle is labeled y = 1 and the bottom side which slopes downward to the right from (0, 1) to (1, 0) is labeled y = 1 minus x. The region within the triangle is shaded and labeled D. A vertical line segment is drawn from the bottom side to the top side and an arrow head placed on the line segment points upward.

example.paragraph: Solution From Equation 2 and Figure 3 we have

$$\begin{array}{l} {Q = {\iint\limits_{D}\sigma}\left( {x,y} \right)dA = {\int_{0}^{1}{\int_{1 - x}^{1}{xy}}}dydx} \\ {\phantom{Q}{= {\int_{0}^{1}\left\lbrack {x\frac{y^{2}}{2}} \right\rbrack}_{y = 1 - x}^{y = 1}dx = {\int_{0}^{1}{\frac{x}{2}{\lbrack{1^{2} - \left( {1 - x} \right)^{2}}\rbrack}}}dx}} \\ {\phantom{Q}{= \frac{1}{2}{\int_{0}^{1}{({2x^{2} - x^{3}})dx}} = \frac{1}{2}\left\lbrack {\frac{2x^{3}}{3} - \frac{x^{4}}{4}} \right\rbrack_{0}^{1} = \frac{5}{24}}} \end{array}$$
Thus the total charge is $$\frac{5}{24}C$$ .

section.heading: Moments and Centers of Mass
section.paragraph: In Section 8.3 we found the center of mass of a lamina with constant density; here we consider a lamina with variable density. Suppose the lamina occupies a region $$D$$ and has density function $$\rho\left( {x,y} \right)$$ . Recall from Chapter 8 that we defined the moment of a particle about an axis as the product of its mass and its directed distance from the axis. We divide $$D$$ into small rectangles as in Figure 2. Then the mass of $$R_{ij}$$ is approximately $$\rho{({x_{ij}^{\ast},y_{ij}^{\ast}})}\Delta A$$ , so we can approximate the moment of $$R_{ij}$$ with respect to the $$x$$ -axis by
$${\lbrack{\rho{({x_{ij,}^{\ast}y_{ij}^{\ast}})}\Delta A}\rbrack}y_{ij}^{\ast}$$
If we now add these quantities and take the limit as the number of subrectangles becomes large, we obtain the moment of the entire lamina about the $$\mathbf{x}$$ -axis:

$$M_{x} = \lim\limits_{m,n\rightarrow\infty}\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{m}\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{n}y_{ij}^{\ast}\rho{({x_{ij}^{\ast},y_{ij}^{\ast}})}\Delta A = {\iint\limits_{D}{y\rho\left( {x,y} \right)dA}}$$
Similarly, the moment about the $$\mathbf{y}$$ -axis is

$$M_{y} = \lim\limits_{m,n\rightarrow\infty}\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{m}\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{n}x_{ij}^{\ast}\rho{({x_{ij}^{\ast},y_{ij}^{\ast}})}\Delta A = {\iint\limits_{D}{x\rho\left( {x,y} \right)dA}}$$

As before, we define the center of mass $$\left( {\overline{x},\overline{y}} \right)$$ so that $$m\overline{x} = M_{y}$$ and $$m\overline{y} = M_{x}$$ . The physical significance is that the lamina behaves as if its entire mass is concentrated at its center of mass. Thus the lamina balances horizontally when supported at its center of mass (see Figure 4).

image.alt: Details A flat solid, labeled D, resembling the sole of a shoe is displayed. A thin tall cone is placed below the solid with its tip touching a point labeled (x bar, y bar) on the broader side of the solid.

section.paragraph: The coordinates $$\left( {\overline{x},\overline{y}} \right)$$ of the center of mass of a lamina occupying the region $$D$$ and having density function $$\rho\left( {x,y} \right)$$ are
$${\overline{x} = \frac{M_{y}}{m} = \frac{1}{m}{\iint\limits_{D}{x\rho\left( {x,y} \right)}}dA} {\overline{y} = \frac{M_{x}}{m} = \frac{1}{m}{\iint\limits_{D}{y\rho\left( {x,y} \right)}}dA}$$
where the mass $$m$$ is given by
$$m = {\iint\limits_{D}{\rho\left( {x,y} \right)dA}}$$

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: Find the mass and center of mass of a triangular lamina with vertices $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ , $$\left( {1,0} \right)$$ , and $$\left( {0,2} \right)$$ if the density function is $$\rho\left( {x,y} \right) = 1 + 3x + y$$ .
Solution The triangle is shown in Figure 5. (Note that the equation of the upper boundary is $$y = 2 - 2x$$ .) The mass of the lamina is

$$\begin{array}{l} {m = {\iint\limits_{D}{\rho\left( {x,y} \right)}}dA = {\int_{0}^{1}{\int_{0}^{2 - 2x}\left( {1 + 3x + y} \right)}}dydx} \\ {\phantom{m} = {\int_{0}^{1}\left\lbrack {y + 3xy + \frac{y^{2}}{2}} \right\rbrack_{y = 0}^{y = 2 - 2x}}dx} \\ {\phantom{m} = 4{\int_{0}^{1}{({1 - x^{2}})}}dx = 4\left\lbrack {x - \frac{x^{3}}{3}} \right\rbrack_{0}^{1} = \frac{8}{3}} \end{array}$$

image.alt: Details A triangular region and a point are graphed in the first quadrant of the x y coordinate plane. The region rests on the x axis with its vertices at (0, 0), (0, 2), and (1, 0). The hypotenuse is labeled y = 2 minus 2 x. The triangular region is labeled D. A point at the center of the triangle is labeled (?, 11/16).

example.paragraph: Then the formulas in (5) give

$$\begin{array}{l} {\overline{x} = \frac{1}{m}{\iint\limits_{D}{x\rho\left( {x,y} \right)}}dA = \frac{3}{8}{\int_{0}^{1}{\int_{0}^{2 - 2x}{({x + 3x^{2} + xy})}}}dydx} \\ {\phantom{\overline{x}} = \frac{3}{8}{\int_{0}^{1}\left\lbrack {xy + 3x^{2}y + x\frac{y^{2}}{2}} \right\rbrack_{y = 0}^{y = 2 - 2x}}dx} \\ {\phantom{\overline{x}} = \frac{3}{2}{\int_{0}^{1}{({x - x^{3}})}}dx = \frac{3}{2}\left\lbrack {\frac{x^{2}}{2} - \frac{x^{4}}{4}} \right\rbrack_{0}^{1} = \frac{3}{8}} \\ {\overline{y} = \frac{1}{m}{\iint\limits_{D}{y\rho\left( {x,y} \right)}}dA = \frac{3}{8}{\int_{0}^{1}{\int_{0}^{2 - 2x}{({y + 3xy + y^{2}})}}}dydx} \\ {\phantom{\overline{y}} = \frac{3}{8}{\int_{0}^{1}\left\lbrack {\frac{y^{2}}{2} + 3x\frac{y^{2}}{2} + \frac{y^{3}}{3}} \right\rbrack_{y = 0}^{y = 2 - 2x}}dx = \frac{1}{4}{\int_{0}^{1}{({7 - 9x - 3x^{2} + 5x^{3}})}}dx} \\ {\phantom{\overline{y}} = \frac{1}{4}\left\lbrack {7x - 9\frac{x^{2}}{2} - x^{3} + 5\frac{x^{4}}{4}} \right\rbrack_{0}^{1} = \frac{11}{16}} \end{array}$$
The center of mass is at the point $$\left( {\frac{3}{8},\frac{11}{16}} \right)$$ .

example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: The density at any point on a semicircular lamina is proportional to the distance from the center of the circle. Find the center of mass of the lamina.

Solution Let’s place the lamina as the upper half of the circle $$x^{2} + y^{2} = a^{2}$$ . (See Figure 6.) Then the distance from a point $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ to the center of the circle (the origin) is $$\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}$$ . Therefore the density function is
$$\rho\left( {x,y} \right) = K\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}$$

where $$K$$ is some constant. Both the density function and the shape of the lamina suggest that we convert to polar coordinates. Then $$\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}} = r$$ and the region $$D$$ is given by $$0 \leqslant r \leqslant a$$ , $$0 \leqslant \theta \leqslant \pi$$ . Thus the mass of the lamina is

$$\begin{array}{l} {m = {\iint\limits_{D}\rho}\left( {x,y} \right)dA = {\iint\limits_{D}{K\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}}}dA} \\ {\phantom{m} = {\int_{0}^{\pi}{\int_{0}^{a}{\left( {Kr} \right)rdrd\theta = K{\int_{0}^{\pi}{d\theta}}{\int_{0}^{a}{r^{2}dr}}}}}} \\ {\phantom{m} = K\pi\left. \frac{r^{3}}{3} \right\rbrack_{0}^{a} = \frac{K\pi a^{3}}{3}} \end{array}$$

image.alt: Details A semicircular region is graphed in the x y coordinate plane. The boundary of the region has a horizontal base along the x axis from (negative a, 0) to (a, 0) and the semicircular arch crosses the y axis at (0, a). The arch is labeled x^2 + y^2 = a. The region within the boundary is shaded and labeled D. A point marked on the y axis is labeled (0, (3 a)/(2 pi)).

example.paragraph: Both the lamina and the density function are symmetric with respect to the $$y$$ -axis, so the center of mass must lie on the $$y$$ -axis, that is, $$\overline{x} = 0$$ . The $$y$$ -coordinate is given by

$$\begin{array}{l} {\overline{y} = \frac{1}{m}{\iint\limits_{D}{y\rho\left( {x,y} \right)dA = \frac{3}{K\pi a^{3}}{\int_{0}^{\pi}{\int_{0}^{a}{r\sin\theta\left( {Kr} \right)rdrd\theta}}}}}} \\ {\phantom{\overline{y}} = \frac{3}{\pi a^{3}}{\int_{0}^{\pi}{\sin\theta d\theta{\int_{0}^{a}r^{3}}dr =}}\frac{3}{\pi a^{3}}\left\lbrack {- \cos\theta} \right\rbrack_{0}^{\pi}\left\lbrack \frac{r^{4}}{4} \right\rbrack_{0}^{a}} \\ {\phantom{\overline{y}} = \frac{3}{\pi a^{3}}\frac{2a^{4}}{4} = \frac{3a}{2\pi}} \end{array}$$
Therefore the center of mass is located at the point $$\left( {0,3a \slash \left( {2\pi} \right)} \right)$$ .

Compare the location of the center of mass in Example 3 with Example 8.3.4, where we found that the center of mass of a lamina with the same shape but uniform density is located at the point $$\left( {0,4a \slash \left( {3\pi} \right)} \right)$$ .

section.heading: Moment of Inertia
section.paragraph: The moment of inertia (also called the second moment) of a particle of mass $$m$$ about an axis is defined to be $$mr^{2}$$ , where $$r$$ is the distance from the particle to the axis. We extend this concept to a lamina with density function $$\rho\left( {x,y} \right)$$ and occupying a region $$D$$ by proceeding as we did for ordinary moments. We divide $$D$$ into small rectangles, approximate the moment of inertia of each subrectangle about the $$x$$ -axis, and take the limit of the sum as the number of subrectangles becomes large. The result is the moment of inertia of the lamina about the $$\mathbf{x}$$ -axis:

$$\begin{array}{l} {I_{x} = \lim\limits_{m,n\rightarrow\infty}\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{m}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{n}{{(y_{ij}^{\ast})}^{2}\rho{({x_{ij}^{\ast},y_{ij}^{\ast}})}\Delta A}}} \\ { = {\iint\limits_{D}{y^{2}\rho\left( {x,y} \right)dA}}} \end{array}$$
Similarly, the moment of inertia about the $$\mathbf{y}$$ -axis is

$$\begin{array}{l} {I_{y} = \lim\limits_{m,n\rightarrow\infty}\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{m}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{n}{{(x_{\mathit{ij}}^{\ast})}^{2}\rho{({x_{\mathit{ij}}^{\ast},y_{\mathit{ij}}^{\ast}})}\Delta A}}} \\ { = {\iint\limits_{D}{x^{2}\rho\left( {x,y} \right)dA}}} \end{array}$$
We also consider the moment of inertia about the origin, also called the polar moment of inertia:

$$I_{0} = \lim\limits_{m,n\rightarrow\infty}\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{m}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{n}{\left\lbrack {{(x_{ij}^{\ast})}^{2} + {(y_{ij}^{\ast})}^{2}} \right\rbrack\rho{({x_{ij}^{\ast},y_{ij}^{\ast}})}\Delta A = {\iint\limits_{D}{{({x^{2} + y^{2}})}\rho\left( {x,y} \right)dA}}}}$$
Note that $$I_{0} = I_{x} + I_{y}$$ .

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: Find the moments of inertia $$I_{x}$$ , $$I_{y}$$ , and $$I_{0}$$ of a homogeneous disk $$D$$ with density $$\rho\left( {x,y} \right) = \rho$$ , center the origin, and radius $$a$$ .

Solution The boundary of $$D$$ is the circle $$x^{2} + y^{2} = a^{2}$$ and in polar coordinates $$D$$ is described by $$0 \leqslant \theta \leqslant 2\pi$$ , $$0 \leqslant r \leqslant a$$ . By Formula 6,

$$\begin{array}{l} {I_{x} = {\iint\limits_{D}{y^{2}\rho dA = \rho{\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\int_{0}^{a}{{(r\sin\theta)}^{2}rdrd\theta}}}}}} \\ {\phantom{I_{x}} = \rho{\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\sin^{2}\theta}d\theta{\int_{0}^{a}r^{3}dr = \rho\int_{0}^{2\pi}\frac{1}{2}(1 - \cos 2\theta})d\theta{\int_{0}^{a}r^{3}dr}}} \\ {\phantom{I_{x}} = \frac{\rho}{2}\left\lbrack \theta - \frac{1}{2}\sin 2\theta \right\rbrack_{0}^{2\pi}\left\lbrack \frac{r^{4}}{4} \right\rbrack_{0}^{a} = \frac{\pi\rho a^{4}}{4}} \end{array}$$
Similarly, Formula 7 gives

$$\begin{array}{l} {I_{y} = {\iint\limits_{D}{x^{2}\rho dA = \rho{\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\int_{0}^{a}{{(r\cos\theta)}^{2}rdrd\theta}}}}}} \\ {\phantom{I_{y}} = \rho\int_{0}^{2\pi}\frac{1}{2}(1 + \cos 2\theta)d\theta\int_{0}^{a}r^{3}dr = \frac{\pi\rho a^{4}}{4}} \end{array}$$
(From the symmetry of the problem, it is expected that $$I_{x} = I_{y}$$ .) We could use Formula 8 to compute $$I_{0}$$ directly, or use

Thus if we increase the mass or the radius of the disk, we thereby increase the moment of inertia. The moment of inertia of a wheel is what makes it difficult to start or stop the rotation of the wheel, just as the mass of a car is what makes it difficult to start or stop the motion of the car.

section.heading: Probability
section.paragraph: In Section 8.5 we considered the probability density function $$f$$ of a continuous random variable $$X$$ . This means that $$f(x) \geqslant 0$$ for all $$x$$ , $$\int_{- \infty}^{\infty}{f{(x)}dx = 1}$$ , and the probability that $$X$$ lies between $$a$$ and $$b$$ is found by integrating $$f$$ from $$a$$ to $$b$$ :
$$P\left( {a \leqslant X \leqslant b} \right) = {\int_{a}^{b}{f(x)dx}}$$

Now we consider a pair of continuous random variables $$X$$ and $$Y$$ , such as the lifetimes of two components of a machine or the height and weight of an adult female chosen at random. The joint density function of $$X$$ and $$Y$$ is a function $$f$$ of two variables such that the probability that $$\left( {X,Y} \right)$$ lies in a region $$D$$ is
$$P\left( {\left( {X,Y} \right) \in D} \right) = {\iint\limits_{D}{f\left( {x,y} \right)dA}}$$
In particular, if the region is a rectangle, then the probability that $$X$$ lies between $$a$$ and $$b$$ and $$Y$$ lies between $$c$$ and $$d$$ is
$$P\left( {a \leqslant X \leqslant b,c \leqslant Y \leqslant d} \right) = {\int_{a}^{b}{\int_{c}^{d}{f\left( {x,y} \right)dydx}}}$$
(See Figure 7.)

section.paragraph: Because probabilities aren’t negative and are measured on a scale from $$0$$ to $$1$$ , the joint density function has the following properties:
$$f\left( {x,y} \right) \geqslant 0 {\iint\limits_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}{f\left( {x,y} \right)dA = 1}}$$
As in Exercise 15.3.50, the double integral over $${\mathbb{R}}^{2}$$ is an improper integral defined as the limit of double integrals over expanding circles or squares, and we can write
$${\iint\limits_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}{f\left( {x,y} \right)dA}} = {\int_{- \infty}^{\infty}{\int_{- \infty}^{\infty}{f{\left( {x,y} \right)}\mathit{dx}\mathit{dy} = 1}}}$$

example.heading: Example 6
example.paragraph: If the joint density function for $$X$$ and $$Y$$ is given by
$$f\left( {x,y} \right) = \begin{cases} {C\left( {x + 2y} \right)} & {{if}0 \leqslant x \leqslant 10,0 \leqslant y \leqslant 10} \\ 0 & {otherwise} \end{cases}$$
find the value of the constant $$C$$ . Then find $$P\left( {X \leqslant 7,Y \geqslant 2} \right)$$ .

Solution We find the value of $$C$$ by ensuring that the double integral of $$f$$ over $${\mathbb{R}}^{2}$$ is equal to $$1$$ . Because $$f\left( {x,y} \right) = 0$$ outside the rectangle $$\left\lbrack {0,10} \right\rbrack \times \left\lbrack {0,10} \right\rbrack$$ , we have

$$\begin{array}{l} {\int_{- \infty}^{\infty}{\int_{- \infty}^{\infty}{f\left( {x,y} \right)dydx}} = {\int_{0}^{10}{\int_{0}^{10}{C\left( {x + 2y} \right)dydx = C{\int_{0}^{10}\left\lbrack {xy + y^{2}} \right\rbrack_{y = 0}^{y = 10}}}}}dx} \\ {\phantom{\int_{- \infty}^{\infty}{\int_{- \infty}^{\infty}{f\left( {x,y} \right)dydx}}} = C{\int_{0}^{10}{{\left( {10x + 100} \right)}dx = 1500C}}} \end{array}$$
Therefore $$1500C = 1$$ and so $$C = \frac{1}{1500}$$ .
Now we can compute the probability that $$X$$ is at most $$7$$ and $$Y$$ is at least $$2$$ :

$$\begin{array}{l} {P\left( {X \leqslant 7,Y \geqslant 2} \right) = {\int_{- \infty}^{7}{\int_{2}^{\infty}{f\left( {x,y} \right)dydx}}} = {\int_{0}^{7}{\int_{2}^{10}{\frac{1}{1500}\left( {x + 2y} \right)dydx}}}} \\ {\phantom{P\left( {X \leqslant 7,Y > 2} \right)} = \frac{1}{1500}{\int_{0}^{7}\left\lbrack {xy + y^{2}} \right\rbrack}_{y = 2}^{y = 10}dx = \frac{1}{1500}{\int_{0}^{7}{\left( {8x + 96} \right)dx}}} \\ {\phantom{P\left( {X \leqslant 7,Y > 2} \right)} = \frac{868}{1500} \approx 0.5787} \end{array}$$

section.paragraph: Suppose $$X$$ is a random variable with probability density function $$f_{1}(x)$$ and $$Y$$ is a random variable with density function $$f_{2}(y)$$ . Then $$X$$ and $$Y$$ are called independent random variables if their joint density function is the product of their individual density functions:
$$f\left( {x,y} \right) = f_{1}(x)f_{2}(y)$$
In Section 8.5 we modeled waiting times by using exponential density functions
$$f(t) = \begin{cases} 0 & {{if}t < 0} \\ {\mu^{- 1}e^{- t \slash \mu}} & {{if}t \geqslant 0} \end{cases}$$
where $$\mu$$ is the mean waiting time. In the next example we consider a situation with two independent waiting times.

example.heading: Example 7
example.paragraph: The manager of a movie theater determines that the average time moviegoers wait in line to buy a ticket for a film is $$10$$ minutes and the average time they wait to buy popcorn is $$5$$ minutes. Assuming that the waiting times are independent, find the probability that a moviegoer waits a total of less than $$20$$ minutes before taking his or her seat.

Solution Assuming that both the waiting time $$X$$ for the ticket purchase and the waiting time $$Y$$ in the refreshment line are modeled by exponential probability density functions, we can write the individual density functions as

$$f_{1}(x) = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} 0 & {{if}x < 0} \\ {\frac{1}{10}e^{- x \slash 10}} & {{if}x \geqslant 0} \end{array} f_{2}(y) = \begin{cases} 0 & {{if}y < 0} \\ {\frac{1}{5}e^{- y \slash 5}} & {{if}y \geqslant 0} \end{cases} \right.$$
Since $$X$$ and $$Y$$ are independent, the joint density function is the product:
$$f(x,y) = f_{1}(x)f_{2}(y) = \begin{cases} {\frac{1}{50}{e^{- x \slash 10}e^{- y \slash 5}}} & {{if}x \geqslant 0,y \geqslant 0} \\ 0 & {otherwise} \end{cases}$$
We are asked for the probability that $$X + Y < 20$$ :
$$P\left( {X + Y < 20} \right) = P\left( {\left( {X,Y} \right) \in D} \right)$$
where $$D$$ is the triangular region shown in Figure 8. Thus

$$\begin{array}{l} {P\left( {X + Y < 20} \right) = {\iint\limits_{D}{f\left( {x,y} \right)dA}} = {\int_{0}^{20}{\int_{0}^{20 - x}{\frac{1}{50}e^{- x \slash 10}e^{- y \slash 5}dydx}}}} \\ {\phantom{P\left( {X + Y < 20} \right)} = \frac{1}{50}\int_{0}^{20}\left\lbrack {e^{- x \slash 10}\left( {- 5} \right)e^{- y \slash 5}} \right\rbrack_{y = 0}^{y = 20 - x}dx} \\ {\phantom{P{({X + Y < 20})}} = \frac{1}{10}{\int_{0}^{20}{e^{- x \slash 10}{({1 - e^{{({x - 20})} \slash 5}})}dx}}} \\ {\phantom{P{({X + Y < 20})}} = \frac{1}{10}{\int_{0}^{20}{{({e^{- x \slash 10} - e^{- 4}e^{ x \slash 10}})}dx}}} \\ {\phantom{P\left( {X + Y < 20} \right)} = 1 + e^{- 4} - 2e^{- 2} \approx 0.7476} \end{array}$$

section.heading: Expected Values
section.paragraph: Recall from Section 8.5 that if $$X$$ is a random variable with probability density function $$f$$ , then its mean is
$$\mu = {\int_{- \infty}^{\infty}{xf(x)dx}}$$
Now if $$X$$ and $$Y$$ are random variables with joint density function $$f$$ , we define the $$\mathbf{X}$$ -mean and $$\mathbf{Y}$$ -mean, also called the expected values of $$X$$ and $$Y$$ , to be
$${\mu_{1} = {\iint\limits_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}{xf\left( {x,y} \right)dA}}} {\mu_{2} = {\iint\limits_{{\mathbb{R}}^{2}}{yf\left( {x,y} \right)dA}}}$$

Notice how closely the expressions for $$\mu_{1}$$ and $$\mu_{2}$$ in (11) resemble the moments $$M_{x}$$ and $$M_{y}$$ of a lamina with density function $$\rho$$ in Equations 3 and 4. In fact, we can think of probability as being like continuously distributed mass. We calculate probability the way we calculate mass—by integrating a density function. And because the total “probability mass” is $$1$$ , the expressions for $$\overline{x}$$ and $$\overline{y}$$ in (5) show that we can think of the expected values of $$X$$ and $$Y$$ , $$\mu_{1}$$ and $$\mu_{2}$$ , as the coordinates of the “center of mass” of the probability distribution.
